newsitem.title: USA: SmithKline gets U.S. FDA okay on Infanrix.
newsitem.headline: SmithKline gets U.S. FDA okay on Infanrix.

text.p: SmithKline Beecham said Thursday the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had granted a license to SmithKline Beecham Biologicals to manufacture Infanrix for immunization against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (whooping cough).
The vaccine for infants and children six weeks to seven years of age will be distributed by SmithKline Beecham Pharmaceuticals.

Infanrix, which contains three pertussis antigens -- pertactin, pertussis toxoid and filamentous hemagglutinin -- demonstrated an absolute efficacy of 89 percent in preventing pertussis in a German household contact study, SmithKline said.
Infanrix also includes antigens to protect against diphtheria and tetanus.
SmithKline is the exclusive license holder of the pertactin antigen from Evans Medical Ltd, a subsidiary of Medeva Plc .
Infanrix demonstrated a superior safety profile as compared to that of whole-cell DTP vaccines, it said.
Whole-cell vaccines, although effective, are associated with relatively high rates of side effects.
Acellular vaccines such as Infanrix cause significantly fewer local and systemic reactions, the company said.
Infanrix has been licensed in more than 10 countries, including Germany, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland, Belgium and Greece.
